title: How fast
hookLine: in the commentaries, many mind-moments pass while one moment of matter lasts

cards: There's a short passage in the Buddha's discourses that sounds almost like a shrug. He says he can't think of anything that changes as quickly as the mind.

So quickly, he adds, that it isn't easy to find a comparison for it. No number, no measurement, just a teacher admitting that the mind outruns his similes. The Abhidhamma and its commentaries didn't leave it there.
They tried to measure it anyway.

teach.b: Start with the smallest unit. A moment of mind, a khana, has three phases: it arises, it stands, it dissolves. Then the next one arises.
In this picture, nothing in between holds still long enough to be a self watching from the side. Each moment does its one job and is gone. Now set matter beside it.
Matter also arises and passes, but more slowly: one moment of matter, the manual says, lasts as long as seventeen moments of mind.
So while one moment of matter in your hand comes and goes, a whole run of mental moments has arisen, seen, felt and vanished. Now a blink.

In the time it takes the eyelids to close and open, tradition says, a great many mind-moments pass. Some later teachers reach for huge numbers, and those can be held loosely. The point isn't the arithmetic.

teach.h: A BLINK IS A CROWD OF MOMENTS.
teach.b: It's the direction: whatever you call this second is already a crowd of moments, each gone before you could name it. Why measure at all? Because of the Buddha's shrug.
If nothing changes as quickly as the mind, nothing you're feeling right now is going to stay. A sharp word, a craving, a wave of fear: by the time you notice it, it's already becoming something else.
The speed isn't meant to make you dizzy. It's meant to loosen the grip.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the three phases of a mind-moment and the manual's comparison of mind-moments to moments of matter, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to notice how quickly experience changes.

the Buddha said it isn't easy to find a simile for how fast the mind changes

games.q: you blink, and the room is still there, apparently unchanged. by the manual's account, what happened during the blink?
o: a great many mind-moments arose and passed
games.why: tradition says a great many mind-moments pass in a blink; whatever you call this second is already a crowd of moments.

practice: Rest your open eyes on something nearby, then blink once, slowly, and notice the light going, the dark, and the light returning, and how the thing you were looking at seems to be waiting there, unchanged.
Then let the breath carry you, and each time you remember, blink once more and watch the whole small drama happen.

wordCard.voice: How fast. In the manual, one moment of matter lasts while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass, and a blink holds a great many. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: a moment, the smallest unit of mind, which arises, stands and dissolves.

carryVoice: Your line: faster than a blink. Whatever you're feeling now is already on its way to something else. Rest well.
